reads.title: The four-day week
reads.text:
A growing number of companies are experimenting with a four-day working week. Employees work around thirty-two hours instead of forty, but their salary stays the same.

The results of recent trials have been surprisingly positive. Most workers said they felt less stressed and slept better. Many companies reported that productivity stayed the same or even increased, because people wasted less time in long meetings.

However, the model does not suit every business. Hospitals, shops and restaurants need staff every day, so they would have to hire more people. Critics also worry that some employees might simply squeeze five days of work into four, which could make them more tired, not less.

Still, after the trials ended, more than ninety per cent of the companies decided to continue with the shorter week.

Why did productivity stay the same in many companies?
o: People spent less time in long meetings

reads.title: Why we forget names
reads.text:
Have you ever met someone at a party and forgotten their name thirty seconds later? You are not alone. Psychologists say this happens to almost everyone.

One reason is attention. When we meet a new person, we are often busy thinking about what to say next or how we look, so the name never really enters our memory.

Another reason is that names are arbitrary. A word like 'baker' tells you something about a person, but a name like 'Mark' does not. Our brains find it much easier to remember information that has meaning.

The good news is that there are simple tricks. Repeat the name immediately: 'Nice to meet you, Mark.' Then connect it to something you already know, like a friend with the same name. Finally, use it again at the end of the conversation.

questions.q: According to the text, why do we often not hear names properly?
o: We are thinking about other things

questions.q: Why is 'baker' easier to remember than 'Mark'?

o: Connecting it to someone you know

reads.title: The return of the night train
reads.text:
Ten years ago, night trains in Europe seemed to be heading for extinction. Cheap flights had made them look slow and old-fashioned, and many routes were cut.

Today, the picture is very different. New sleeper services connect cities such as Vienna, Paris, Amsterdam and Budapest, and tickets often sell out weeks in advance. Part of the reason is environmental: a train journey produces a fraction of the emissions of a short-haul flight.

But climate concerns are not the whole story. Travellers say they enjoy falling asleep in one country and waking up in another, without the stress of airport security. For business travellers, an overnight train can also save the cost of a hotel.

The main obstacles are price and comfort. A private compartment can cost more than a plane ticket, and older carriages are cramped. Operators are now investing in modern cabins, hoping that comfort will win over those who still prefer to fly.

They were too expensive to build
Nobody needed to travel at night

questions.q: What advantage for business travellers is mentioned?
o: Saving the cost of a hotel

reads.title: Learning a language as an adult
reads.text:
It is often said that children learn languages more easily than adults. There is some truth in this, especially when it comes to pronunciation: people who start young are more likely to sound like native speakers.

However, adults have important advantages. They already understand how grammar works in their first language, they can use dictionaries and apps, and they usually have clear reasons for learning, such as work or travel. Studies show that, in the early stages, adults actually progress faster than children.

The biggest difference is time. A child may hear a new language for thousands of hours, while an adult often studies for a couple of hours a week. Researchers therefore recommend small daily habits: ten minutes of listening, a few sentences spoken aloud, and regular review of vocabulary.

In short, age matters less than consistency.

reads.title: The paradox of choice
reads.text:
Conventional wisdom holds that more choice makes us happier. If a supermarket offers fifty kinds of jam instead of five, surely every shopper will find exactly what they want.

Yet a famous experiment suggested otherwise. Shoppers who were shown a display of twenty-four jams were far less likely to buy anything than those who saw only six. Faced with too many options, people struggled to decide and often walked away empty-handed.

Psychologists argue that abundant choice carries hidden costs. It raises our expectations, makes us more likely to regret our decision, and shifts the blame onto ourselves when things go wrong: with so many alternatives, a poor outcome feels like our own fault.

That said, later studies have painted a more nuanced picture. The effect appears strongest when options are hard to compare or when we lack clear preferences. Experts who know exactly what they are looking for tend to welcome a wider range.

questions.q: What happened in the jam experiment?
o: Fewer people bought jam when there were more options
More people bought jam when there were more options

questions.q: Which hidden cost of choice is mentioned?
o: We are more likely to regret our decision

questions.q: According to later studies, who welcomes more choice?

reads.title: Remote work and the city
reads.text:
When offices emptied during the pandemic, many commentators predicted the decline of big cities. If people could work from anywhere, why would they pay high rents to live close to the office?

The reality has turned out to be more complicated. Some workers did move to smaller towns, attracted by cheaper housing and more space. Yet most major cities have retained their appeal, largely because of what they offer outside working hours: culture, restaurants, and the chance to meet new people.

What has changed is the rhythm of city life. City-centre cafés and sandwich shops that depended on office workers are struggling, especially on Mondays and Fridays, when fewer people commute. Meanwhile, residential neighbourhoods have seen a boom in local businesses.

Urban planners are now debating how to repurpose half-empty office buildings. Converting them into flats is one option, but it is expensive and technically challenging, so progress has been slow.

questions.q: Why have most big cities kept their appeal?
o: Because of what they offer outside work
City-centre cafés that served office workers

questions.q: Why is converting offices into flats slow?
o: It is expensive and technically difficult
